candidate.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide immunization education, promote preventive health practices, and reinforce age- and risk-appropriate vaccination.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — vaccine-preventable disease education
candidate.educational_objective: Explain that vaccination has substantially reduced vaccine-preventable disease burden, but continued age- and risk-appropriate vaccination and surveillance remain necessary to preserve protection and prevent resurgence.

options.A: Vaccination has prevented large numbers of illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths, and staying up to date remains important because vaccine-preventable diseases can persist or reemerge when protection is insufficient.
options.B: Successful vaccination programs eliminate the need for continued immunization once disease incidence becomes low.
options.C: Vaccines are relevant mainly to diseases that no longer circulate and therefore provide little current public-health benefit.
options.D: Once a vaccine-preventable disease is controlled locally, surveillance and continued vaccination are unnecessary.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. CDC reports that routine childhood vaccination has prevented hundreds of millions of illnesses and millions of hospitalizations and deaths in the United States. CDC also emphasizes that serious vaccine-preventable diseases remain a threat and that continued vaccination is needed to maintain protection and prevent reemergence or outbreaks. B and D ignore the need to sustain coverage after disease control or elimination targets are reached. C is false because multiple vaccine-preventable diseases continue to circulate and cause morbidity and mortality.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Vaccines have substantially reduced disease burden and saved lives, but ongoing recommended vaccination and surveillance remain necessary because vaccine-preventable diseases persist and can reemerge when coverage declines.
candidate.source_document_title: Vaccines and the Diseases they Prevent; Vaccine-Preventable Diseases — Global Immunization; Routine Immunizations on Schedule for Everyone (RISE)
candidate.source_locator: Vaccines and the Diseases they Prevent — routine vaccinations for children born 1994–2023 are estimated to prevent about 508 million illnesses, 32 million hospitalizations, and over 1.1 million deaths. Global Immunization — elimination/control sections: continued disease detection and vaccination are required to maintain elimination targets and prevent reemergence. RISE — routine immunization coverage remains an active public-health priority to protect against vaccine-preventable disease and disability.
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
